CHAPTER 7: GOVERNMENT INTERVENTION IN THE MARKET

INTRODUCTION
- The government influences price and quantity outcomes in certain markets.
- Example: without government intervention, cigarettes could cost around 3 euro a packet instead of 14 euro (2021) and would be widely consumed.
- Methods of intervention: taxation, incentives, regulation and legislation.

ECONOMIC SYSTEMS
- Economic system: how resources are allocated and economic decisions are made in an economy.
- North Korea: the government plays a central role in deciding what to produce. US: private individuals make the key decisions.
- Command economy (centrally planned economy), in theory:
- Almost all factors of production owned by the state.
- Maximum government interference - the government controls all economic activity.
- Decision-making is centralised - the state decides what to produce and allocates resources.
- Individuals are selfless and work for the common good (the good of the state).
- Free enterprise (capitalist) economy, in theory:
- Almost all factors of production privately owned.
- Minimal government interference - government supplies public goods, provides national security and passes legislation.
- Entrepreneurs and owners of firms decide what to produce; resources are allocated through the price mechanism.
- Self-interest is the key motivator: utility maximisation for consumers, profit maximisation for firms.
- Mixed economy: in between the two extremes; goods and services are provided by both the state and private individuals/firms. Ireland is an example.
- In a mixed economy the government influences activity through policies, the tax system, incentives, regulation and legislation.

ROLE OF THE GOVERNMENT IN A MIXED ECONOMY
- Economic aims: full employment, economic growth, infrastructure (motorways, ports), balanced regional development, redistribution of income (through tax and social welfare).
- Provides essential services that private firms would not provide to all citizens, e.g. education, healthcare, public goods.
- State-owned firms provide essential services that may be loss-making or need large capital, e.g. train services, rural bus services.
- Regulates markets so firms act in the interest of customers, taxpayers and society.
- Passes legislation, e.g. environmental laws on pollution; laws against anti-competitive behaviour such as price fixing and collusion.
- Intervenes in markets:
- (i) Taxes fossil fuels and plastic bags for environmental reasons; taxes tobacco, alcohol and sugar-sweetened drinks for health reasons.
- (ii) Incentivises supply and demand of certain goods, e.g. subsidies for electric vehicles (EVs); price floors to encourage supply.
- (iii) Intervenes where equilibrium price is too high, e.g. Rent Pressure Zones limit rent increases (Chapter 4).

WHY THE GOVERNMENT INTERVENES IN MARKETS
- To ensure fair prices for consumers, especially for essential goods - e.g. a price ceiling if the market price is too high.
- To ensure fair prices for suppliers - e.g. a price floor gives a guaranteed minimum price.
- To discourage consumption/production of demerit goods.
- Demerit good: a good that can have a negative effect on the consumer and, if over-consumed or over-produced, imposes negative external costs (externalities) on third parties.
- Externality: the external costs (or benefits) that fall on other individuals or society as a result of production or consumption.
- Negative production externalities: meat and dairy production releasing methane (a greenhouse gas); carbon emissions from air travel.
- Negative consumption externalities: consumption of petrol, diesel, coal and home-heating oil producing carbon; excessive alcohol consumption harming the health and justice systems (e.g. Gardai patrolling on a Saturday night).
- To encourage producers to supply particular goods - e.g. the Help to Buy scheme pushed up house prices, which incentivised builders to build more.
- To protect taxpayers - e.g. failure to regulate retail banking in the past cost taxpayers hugely (Chapters 1 and 15).
- To ensure consumers are not exploited - dominant firms must not abuse market power; price fixing and collusive tendering are illegal (Chapter 8).
- To provide essential services private operators might not - e.g. Bus Eireann, Dublin Bus and Irish Rail run loss-making routes.
- To protect the environment - laws on pollution, litter and waste management.

TAXATION (TABLE 7.3)
- Governments tax to raise revenue, but tax is also used for other aims.
- Using tax to INCENTIVISE economic activity:
- Low corporation tax incentivises FDI (Foreign Direct Investment) in Ireland.
- High DIRT (Deposit Interest Retention Tax) encourages spending rather than saving, increasing consumer spending.
- The 2020 'staycation' tax rebate encouraged domestic tourism when hospitality was struggling.
- The 'bike to work' scheme encourages people to buy bikes, reducing traffic congestion and pressure on public transport and encouraging healthier lifestyles.
- Using tax to INFLUENCE CONSUMER BEHAVIOUR:
- VAT and excise duty on tobacco and alcohol discourage smoking and drinking.
- Excise duty, VAT and carbon taxes discourage fossil fuel use and encourage public transport.
- The sugar-sweetened drinks tax discourages unhealthy drinks and makes substitutes such as water more attractive.
- VAT in hospitality was cut from 13.5% to 9% in 2020/2021 so firms could cut prices to attract customers.

EXAMPLE 1: SUGAR-SWEETENED DRINKS TAX
- Introduced in 2018 (same time as the UK).
- Reduces consumption of sugary drinks, particularly by children.
- Reduces future burden on the health system if obesity, diabetes and tooth decay fall.
- Healthier drinks (water, low/no sugar drinks) become relatively more attractive.
- Incentivises producers to make drinks healthier to avoid the tax - but some replaced sugar with sweeteners that are also unhealthy.
- Fall in demand could affect employment in drinks companies.
- Revenue could fund healthy lifestyle initiatives, e.g. sports equipment for schools (done in other countries).

EXAMPLE 2: CARBON EMISSIONS AND THE CARBON TAX
- Carbon tax: a charge applied to carbon-emitting fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas.
- Expected to reach 100 euro per tonne of carbon by 2030; makes petrol, diesel, home-heating oil, gas, coal and briquettes more expensive, encouraging a switch to greener alternatives.
- Government aims for close to 1 million EVs on Irish roads by 2030. In 2021 up to 10,000 euro in subsidies and tax rebates were available towards buying an EV.
- Motor tax on EVs in 2021: reduced rate of 120 euro; higher for petrol/diesel cars, expected to increase.
- Implications of increasing the carbon tax:
- Demand for fossil fuels should fall, reducing emissions that cause climate change.
- Greener alternatives become relatively more attractive (public transport, EVs, solar panels).
- Electricity demand will rise sharply with 1 million EVs; generating capacity and renewable energy must increase.
- Rural dwellers are disproportionately affected, as they have fewer public transport options.
- Carbon tax is regressive - it does not take account of ability to pay.
- Unemployment will rise among fossil fuel industry workers.
- Government current revenue will fall, as indirect taxes on fossil fuels are a major source; an alternative indirect tax will be needed.
- Other actions to reduce carbon emissions: restricting turf cutting (bogs absorb carbon); closing high-carbon power stations (ESB closed peat plants at Lanesboro and Shannonbridge in 2020); planting trees (Climate Action Plan: 440 million trees by 2040); higher VRT and motor tax on petrol/diesel cars.

EXAMPLE 3: PLASTIC BAG LEVY
- Environmental levy on plastic bags introduced in 2002 to reduce their production and consumption.
- Bags now have a monetary value (22c in 2021), so shoppers reuse rather than discard them.
- Consumer behaviour changed: demand at point of sale fell substantially; most shoppers use their own reusable bags ('bag for life').
- Suppliers more likely to supply paper bags (especially clothing retailers).
- Plastic bag litter and landfill dropped; many other countries copied the levy.

EXAMPLE 4: DISPOSABLE NON-RECYCLABLE DRINK CUPS ('LATTE LEVY')
- 200 million disposable coffee cups discarded each year in Ireland by 2020 (source: mywaste.ie).
- Proposed 'latte levy' would raise the price of a takeaway drink in a disposable cup by up to 25c.
- Implications: higher price lowers demand, reducing waste; encourages reusable 'keep cups'; possible loss of sales for coffee shops; revenue could fund environmental initiatives (e.g. tree planting); could close businesses such as disposable cup manufacturers.

EXAMPLE 5: RESIDENTIAL PROPERTY - HELP TO BUY
- Expanded at end of 2020 to 10% of the purchase price of a newly built property, up to a maximum of 30,000 euro, for qualifying first-time buyers.
- Main priority was not helping buyers. It was a response to Central Bank restrictions on mortgage size.
- Those restrictions limited what buyers could pay, so builders were reluctant to build (supply) homes.
- The payment let buyers secure a bigger mortgage and pay more, reassuring builders they could charge higher prices, incentivising them to build more.

EXAMPLE 6: MINIMUM UNIT PRICING OF ALCOHOL
- Low off-licence and supermarket prices are a major contributor to excessive drinking.
- Negative externalities: costs to the health system (treating those who drink to excess or are injured); costs to the justice system (policing, courts, prisons - drink-driving, violence, vandalism).
- Government plans to introduce it at the same time as Northern Ireland to deter cross-border shopping.
- Minimum price linked to the number of alcohol units in the drink - more units, higher minimum price.
- Does not affect pubs, restaurants or hotels; targets cheap alcohol in off-licences and supermarkets.
- It is NOT a tax - it is a minimum price the seller must charge.
- Actions already taken (Table 7.4): ban on alcohol ads on public transport, bus stops and stations; near schools, creches and playgrounds; in cinemas for films not rated 18; alcohol segregated in supermarkets and not visible behind checkouts; limits on alcohol ads at certain sporting events (2021); no loyalty card points for or on alcohol; HSE support via askaboutalcohol.ie.
- Possible future actions: ban drinks companies sponsoring sport; ban TV alcohol ads before 9pm or all alcohol advertising; raise legal drinking age from 18 to 21 (as in the US); fund publicity campaigns; plain packaging or cigarette-style health warnings on labels.

EXAMPLE 7: CIGARETTES
- Tobacco is heavily taxed and strictly regulated (Chapter 10).
- 2017: Ireland among the first countries to enforce plain packaging, removing the last form of cigarette advertising.
- Figure 7.1: of the 14 euro price for 20 cigarettes (2021), 11 euro (80%) is VAT/excise duty and 3 euro (20%) goes to the manufacturer/distributor.
- The HSE supports smokers who wish to quit.

PRICE CEILINGS
- Price ceiling: a price set below the equilibrium price; suppliers cannot legally charge above it. Used when the equilibrium price is too high.
- Figure 7.2 (in words): price on vertical axis, quantity on horizontal; downward demand and upward supply curves cross at Pe = 30 euro, Qe = 3,000. A horizontal line PMax at 20 euro sits below equilibrium.
- At 30 euro the market clears (3,000 demanded and supplied) but consumers may complain the price is too high.
- Government legislates a ceiling (PMax) of 20 euro; suppliers charging more would be prosecuted.
- Law of Demand: lower price raises quantity demanded to 4,000 (an extra 1,000 consumers enter).
- Law of Supply: lower price (and lower potential profit) cuts quantity supplied to 2,000.
- Result: excess demand of 2,000 units (unsatisfied customers).
- Government may need to ration the good (e.g. to stop stockpiling).
- Producers may be tempted to sell in the hidden/shadow economy above the ceiling.
- Rent ceilings: see Chapter 4.

PRICE FLOORS
- Price floor: a price set above the equilibrium price; a price suppliers are guaranteed to receive. Used to encourage supply and/or ensure producers get enough revenue.
- Figure 7.3 (in words): demand and supply cross at PE = 30 euro, QE = 3,000. A horizontal line PMin at 40 euro sits above equilibrium.
- At 40 euro, Law of Supply: quantity supplied rises to 4,000. Law of Demand: quantity demanded falls to 2,000.
- Result: excess supply (unsold stock) of 2,000 units.
- Government generally buys the unsold stock, stores it or redistributes it (e.g. to an NGO such as a charity).
- Main benefit: suppliers get a guaranteed minimum price.
- Used in agriculture in the past so farmers get a guaranteed minimum revenue and avoid income falls when market prices fall.
- Minimum wage is a price floor: the worker is the supplier, and the minimum wage is above the equilibrium wage. Raising it encourages people to supply labour (e.g. in a labour shortage) and ensures workers receive sufficient income (Chapter 9).

REGULATION
- A regulator is like a referee: it enforces laws and punishes breaches; it can issue orders and fines and bring prosecutions, and can encourage firms to improve behaviour.
- Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC): prevents exploitation through anti-competitive behaviour (price fixing, dividing up sales territories/markets).
- Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI): enforces food hygiene and safety, e.g. in restaurants and delicatessens.
- Health and Safety Authority (HSA): enforces workplace safety laws.
- Environmental Protection Agency (EPA): enforces laws so firms do not damage the environment.
- Central Bank regulates financial institutions (Chapter 15); poor bank regulation in the Celtic Tiger period harmed the state (Chapter 1).

rows.prompt: In a command economy, who owns almost all the factors of production?
rows.explanation: In a command (centrally planned) economy almost all factors of production are owned by the state.

rows.prompt: In a free enterprise economy, resources are allocated mainly through:
rows.explanation: Private individuals decide what to produce and the price mechanism allocates resources.

rows.prompt: In a free enterprise economy, the key motivator for firms is:
options: Working for the good of the state
rows.explanation: Self-interest drives decisions: profit maximisation for firms, utility maximisation for consumers.

rows.prompt: Why do state-owned firms such as Irish Rail provide some services?
options: The services are essential but may be loss-making
Private firms are banned from transport
The services always earn supernormal profit
The EU requires all transport to be state-owned
rows.explanation: The state provides essential services that may be loss-making or need large amounts of capital.

rows.prompt: Rent Pressure Zones are an example of the government intervening because:
options: The equilibrium price is too low
There is excess supply of housing
The equilibrium price is too high
rows.explanation: Rent Pressure Zones limit rent increases where rents are rising.

rows.prompt: A demerit good is one that:
options: Is provided free of charge by the state
Can harm the consumer and impose external costs on others
Benefits everyone who did not buy it
Has no effect on third parties
rows.explanation: Over-consumption of demerit goods harms the consumer and third parties.

rows.prompt: Methane released from meat and dairy production is an example of:
rows.explanation: The external cost arises from producing the goods.

rows.prompt: The cost of extra policing due to excessive drinking is an example of:
rows.explanation: The cost to third parties arises from consuming alcohol.

rows.prompt: Making price fixing and collusive tendering illegal mainly aims to:
rows.explanation: The government ensures dominant firms do not abuse their market power.

rows.prompt: Which tax policy incentivises Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in Ireland?
rows.explanation: Low corporation tax attracts foreign firms to invest in Ireland.

rows.prompt: A high rate of DIRT encourages people to:
options: Save money rather than spend it
Spend money rather than save it
rows.explanation: DIRT is a tax on deposit interest, so a high rate makes saving less attractive.

rows.prompt: In 2020/2021 the VAT rate in the hospitality sector was cut from:
rows.explanation: The cut let hospitality firms lower prices to attract customers.

rows.prompt: The 'bike to work' scheme is an example of using tax to:
options: Incentivise a type of economic activity
rows.explanation: It encourages people to buy bikes, reducing congestion and improving health.

rows.prompt: In what year was the sugar-sweetened drinks tax introduced in Ireland?
rows.explanation: It was introduced in 2018, at the same time as in the UK.

rows.prompt: Which is a possible NEGATIVE effect of the sugar-sweetened drinks tax?
options: Less pressure on the health system
rows.explanation: If demand for sugary drinks falls, employment in drinks companies may be affected.

rows.prompt: The carbon tax is expected to reach what level by 2030?
rows.explanation: The chapter states it is expected to be 100 euro per tonne by 2030.

rows.prompt: Why is the carbon tax described as regressive?
options: It takes a larger share from high earners
It only applies to large companies
It does not take account of the taxpayer's ability to pay
rows.explanation: Everyone pays the same tax on fuel, regardless of income.

rows.prompt: Why are rural dwellers disproportionately affected by the carbon tax?
options: They pay a higher rate of carbon tax
They have fewer public transport options
rows.explanation: Urban dwellers can switch to public transport more easily.

rows.prompt: If the carbon tax succeeds in cutting fossil fuel use, what happens to government current revenue?
options: It rises because the tax rate is higher
It falls, so a new indirect tax source is needed
It stays the same because EVs are taxed
It rises because electricity demand grows
rows.explanation: Indirect taxes on fossil fuels are a major revenue source, so lower use means less revenue.

rows.prompt: The plastic bag levy was introduced in:
rows.explanation: The environmental levy on plastic bags was introduced in 2002.

rows.prompt: Why did the plastic bag levy change consumer behaviour?
options: Bags now have a monetary value, so people reuse them
rows.explanation: Paying for each bag (22c in 2021) made shoppers reuse bags.

rows.prompt: The proposed 'latte levy' would raise the price of a takeaway drink in a disposable cup by up to:
rows.explanation: The levy would add up to 25c to drinks served in disposable cups.

rows.prompt: What was the main priority of the Help to Buy scheme?
options: To incentivise builders to supply more homes
To lower house prices for all buyers
To reduce the size of mortgages
To replace Central Bank mortgage rules
rows.explanation: Higher prices buyers could pay reassured builders and incentivised them to build.

rows.prompt: Minimum unit pricing of alcohol is mainly targeted at:
options: Drinks sold in pubs and hotels
Cheap alcohol in off-licences and supermarkets
rows.explanation: It will not affect pubs, restaurants or hotels.

rows.prompt: Which statement about minimum unit pricing of alcohol is correct?
options: It is a new excise duty
It applies a flat price to all drinks
It is a minimum price, not a tax
rows.explanation: The price is linked to alcohol units and is a price sellers must charge, not a tax.

rows.prompt: Of the 14 euro price of 20 cigarettes in 2021, how much was VAT and excise duty?
rows.explanation: 11 euro (80%) is tax; 3 euro (20%) goes to the manufacturer/distributor.

rows.prompt: A price ceiling is set:
rows.explanation: It is a maximum price suppliers can legally charge, set below equilibrium.

rows.prompt: Equilibrium is 30 euro and 3,000 units. A 20 euro ceiling gives demand of 4,000 and supply of 2,000. The result is:
rows.explanation: 4,000 demanded minus 2,000 supplied = 2,000 units of excess demand.

rows.prompt: A price floor above equilibrium usually leads to:
rows.explanation: Higher price raises supply and lowers demand, leaving unsold stock.

rows.prompt: Which is an example of a price floor?
rows.explanation: The minimum wage is the lowest 'price' an employer must pay, set above the equilibrium wage.

rows.prompt: Which body enforces hygiene standards in restaurants?
options: The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI)
rows.explanation: The FSAI enforces food hygiene and safety.

rows.prompt: Which regulator deals with anti-competitive behaviour such as price fixing?
rows.explanation: The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission deals with anti-competitive behaviour.

rows.prompt: Distinguish between a command economy and a free enterprise economy.
rows.model_answer: In a command economy almost all factors of production are owned by the state, which controls all economic activity and decides what to produce. In a free enterprise economy almost all factors are privately owned, government interference is minimal, and entrepreneurs decide what to produce, with resources allocated by the price mechanism.

rows.prompt: Explain what is meant by the statement 'Ireland is a mixed economy'.
rows.model_answer: A mixed economy lies between a command and a free enterprise economy. In Ireland goods and services are provided by both the state (e.g. education, healthcare, Irish Rail) and private firms, and the government influences activity using taxes, incentives, regulation and legislation.

rows.prompt: Explain the term 'demerit good' and give one example of a negative production externality and one of a negative consumption externality.
rows.model_answer: A demerit good can have a negative effect on the consumer and, if over-consumed or over-produced, imposes external costs on third parties. A negative production externality is methane from meat and dairy production. A negative consumption externality is the cost to the health and justice systems of excessive alcohol consumption.

rows.prompt: Give two examples of the government using the tax system to encourage economic activity and two examples of using it to discourage consumption.
rows.model_answer: Encourage: low corporation tax attracts FDI; the 'bike to work' scheme encourages people to buy bikes (also the staycation rebate, high DIRT). Discourage: VAT and excise duty on tobacco and alcohol; the sugar-sweetened drinks tax (also carbon tax on fossil fuels).

rows.prompt: Explain how the Help to Buy scheme incentivised builders to construct more properties.
rows.model_answer: Central Bank limits on mortgage size meant buyers could not pay high prices, so builders were reluctant to build. Help to Buy gave first-time buyers up to 10% of the price (maximum 30,000 euro) of a new home, letting them get a bigger mortgage and pay more. This reassured builders they could charge higher prices, so they built more.

rows.prompt: State five methods the government could use to reduce alcohol consumption.
rows.model_answer: Minimum unit pricing of alcohol in off-licences and supermarkets; banning drinks companies from sponsoring sport; banning TV alcohol ads before 9pm or all alcohol advertising; raising the legal drinking age from 18 to 21; plain packaging or cigarette-style health warnings on labels (also funding publicity campaigns).

rows.prompt: Explain, with a diagram described in words, what happens when a price floor is set above the equilibrium price.
rows.model_answer: Demand slopes down and supply slopes up, crossing at 30 euro and 3,000 units; a horizontal PMin line is drawn at 40 euro. At 40 euro supply rises to 4,000 and demand falls to 2,000, giving excess supply of 2,000 units. The government usually buys the unsold stock and stores or redistributes it, while suppliers get a guaranteed minimum price.

rows.prompt: Name three regulators in Ireland and state what each one does.
rows.model_answer: The CCPC prevents anti-competitive behaviour such as price fixing. The FSAI enforces food hygiene and safety standards. The HSA enforces workplace safety laws, and the EPA enforces environmental laws.

rows.prompt: Consumers complain that the market price of a good is too high. The government introduces a price ceiling below the equilibrium price. Explain, with the aid of a diagram, the economic implications of this price ceiling. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Diagram (in words): price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal; a downward-sloping demand curve and an upward-sloping supply curve cross at Pe (30 euro) and Qe (3,000). A horizontal line PMax is drawn at 20 euro, below Pe, with Qs (2,000) and Qd (4,000) marked. Implications: 1. Excess demand: due to the Law of Demand, quantity demanded rises to 4,000 as extra consumers enter, while due to the Law of Supply, suppliers offer only 2,000 as potential profits fall, leaving 2,000 unsatisfied customers. 2. Rationing: the government may need to ration the good so it is available to as many consumers as possible and to prevent stockpiling. 3. Shadow economy: producers may be tempted to sell the good in the hidden economy at a price above the ceiling. 4. Lower price for those who obtain it: consumers who get the good pay a fairer price, which is the aim, and suppliers charging more can be prosecuted.
rows.marking_scheme: Diagram 8 marks: axes 2m, D and S curves 2m, equilibrium 2m, PMax below Pe with Qs and Qd 2m. Implications: 3 points x 4 marks (2 marks statement + 2 marks explanation) = 12m. Total 20 marks.

rows.prompt: Discuss the economic implications for Ireland of increasing the carbon tax. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: 1. Lower demand for fossil fuels: taxing diesel, petrol, home-heating oil and coal raises their price, so demand falls and carbon emissions that cause climate change fall. 2. Greener alternatives become more attractive: public transport, EVs and solar panels become relatively cheaper. 3. Higher demand for electricity: with close to 1 million EVs planned by 2030, generating capacity and renewable energy must increase. 4. Rural dwellers are disproportionately affected, as they have fewer public transport options. 5. The tax is regressive, as it ignores ability to pay. 6. Unemployment may rise in the fossil fuel industry. 7. Government current revenue falls, as fossil fuel taxes are a major source of indirect tax, so an alternative source must be found.
rows.marking_scheme: 4 points x 5 marks (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation). Total 20 marks.

rows.prompt: State and explain two reasons why the government might use the tax system other than to raise revenue. Give an example of each. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: 1. To incentivise certain economic activity: e.g. low corporation tax encourages Foreign Direct Investment into Ireland, creating jobs. 2. To discourage consumption of certain goods: e.g. the sugar-sweetened drinks tax raises the price of sugary drinks, reducing consumption and making healthier drinks such as water more attractive.
rows.marking_scheme: 2 points x 5 marks (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation with example). Total 10 marks.

rows.prompt: Outline five reasons why the government intervenes in markets in a mixed economy. (25 marks)
rows.model_answer: 1. To ensure fair prices for consumers, especially for essentials, e.g. a price ceiling if the market price is too high. 2. To ensure fair prices for suppliers, e.g. a price floor guaranteeing farmers a minimum price. 3. To discourage demerit goods that impose negative externalities, e.g. taxes on tobacco, alcohol and sugary drinks. 4. To encourage producers to supply particular goods, e.g. the Help to Buy scheme incentivised builders to build more homes. 5. To protect taxpayers, e.g. poor regulation of banking in the past cost taxpayers hugely. 6. To ensure consumers are not exploited, e.g. price fixing and collusive tendering are illegal. 7. To provide essential services private firms might not, e.g. loss-making Bus Eireann routes. 8. To protect the environment through laws on pollution, litter and waste.
rows.marking_scheme: 5 points x 5 marks (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation/example). Total 25 marks.

rows.prompt: Explain what is meant by minimum unit pricing of alcohol and outline two reasons the government plans to introduce it. (15 marks)
rows.model_answer: Minimum unit pricing links the lowest price a retailer can charge for a drink to the number of alcohol units it contains: the more units, the higher the minimum price. It targets cheap alcohol in off-licences and supermarkets, not pubs, restaurants or hotels, and it is not a tax. Reasons: 1. Low prices in off-licences and supermarkets are a major cause of excessive drinking, so a higher minimum price should reduce consumption. 2. To reduce negative externalities: excessive drinking costs the health system (treating injuries and illness) and the justice system (policing, courts and prisons for drink-driving, violence and vandalism). It is planned at the same time as Northern Ireland to deter cross-border shopping.
rows.marking_scheme: Explanation 5m (link to units 3m + targeted at off-licences/supermarkets or not a tax 2m). Reasons: 2 x 5m (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation). Total 15 marks.
